For small businesses in the DACH region, a website is often perceived as a one-time purchase: order it, launch it, update it occasionally. In practice, it is an operational asset with a cost of ownership, risks associated with changes, legal dependencies, and the question of how to exit the relationship with a contractor.

- Economic predictability is not the same as the lowest price. Cheap hosting or a website builder can be rational for a simple task. But if hacked plugins, undocumented code, manual editing of dozens of pages, and dependence on a single provider appear later, the initial price no longer fully describes the costs. A business needs not only a monthly invoice, but also a map of future obligations.

- An infrastructure-based approach changes what is being purchased. The owner receives not just a visual shell, but a system: where prices, company details, addresses, texts, semantics, design rules, and the release process are stored. This reduces the likelihood that changing one detail will create inconsistencies in other sections. For a craft or service business, this discipline may be more important than additional visual capabilities.

- GDPR/DSGVO, accessibility, and integration issues cannot be resolved with a single technical phrase. Architecture can reduce some of the risks: EU orientation, less unnecessary runtime, control over forms, and a careful structure. But legal review and accessibility audits remain separate tasks. A mature position is precisely not to conflate engineering preparation with formal compliance.

Do you consider a small business website a marketing expense or part of the company’s operational infrastructure?
